summary: This Experimental document defines a BFD Optimized Authentication Mode called Meticulous Keyed ISAAC. It authenticates some BFD packets with less CPU time than MD5 or SHA-1, at a cost in security. It cannot signal state changes but can keep a session in the Up state.

eli5.summary: A cheaper, quicker secret check for routine "I'm still here" messages, good enough for routine ones but not for big news.

questions: why does bfd use isaac for authentication
subtitle: A cheap secret-number check that lets BFD keep a link marked Up without hashing every packet.

tldr.problem: BFD authentication with MD5 or SHA-1 hashes is secure but expensive on resource-constrained hardware, especially when packets arrive hundreds of times per second.
tldr.mechanism: Each packet that merely confirms the session is still Up carries a 32-bit number from an ISAAC pseudorandom stream seeded by a shared secret key, a random Seed and the Your Discriminator value. Changes of state still use full MD5 or SHA-1 authentication.
tldr.outcome: Routine Up packets can be checked at near-zero cost, at the price of weaker security: the packet itself is not authenticated, and the RFC calls ISAAC tolerable here and unsuitable for any other IETF protocol.

facts.label: Secret key length
facts.value: at least 8 octets, SHOULD NOT exceed 128

today: RFC 9986 is an Experimental document published in June 2026; it is not on the Standards Track and the unit metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it. It builds on RFC 9985, and IANA has assigned Auth Types 7 and 8 and registered a YANG module for it.

sections.title: Why a Cheaper Authentication Mode
sections.content:
Bidirectional Forwarding Detection (BFD, RFC 5880) already defines authentication based on MD5 and SHA-1 hashes. These are secure, but the RFC points out that they are expensive and time-consuming on resource-constrained hardware. Without authentication, an attacker can forge, modify or replay packets and make parties believe a link is down, or up when it is not.

RFC 9985 splits the work: a more computationally intensive method protects significant changes, and a less intensive method covers packets that only confirm the session is in the Up state. RFC 9986 supplies the pieces for that scheme. It reuses MD5 and SHA-1 for the intensive part and adds a new Meticulous Keyed ISAAC format for the light part.

The word "meticulous" means the sequence number goes up by one on every packet sent; "keyed" means a secret key known to both ends is involved. The document is Experimental, so implementations based on it should not be treated as compliant with RFC 5880 or assumed to interoperate.
sections.eli5: Hashing every message is like locking and unlocking a safe each time you wave hello. This RFC lets you just show a quick secret number for waves, and keep the safe for important messages.

sections.title: The ISAAC Authentication Section
sections.content:
The new Auth Types are 7 (Optimized MD5 Meticulous Keyed ISAAC) and 8 (Optimized SHA-1 Meticulous Keyed ISAAC). The Optimized Authentication Mode field says which flavour a packet uses: 1 means the full MD5 or SHA-1 format, and 2 means the light ISAAC format.

In the ISAAC format the Authentication Section is 16 bytes. After the Auth Type, Auth Len, Auth Key ID and Opt. Mode fields come a 32-bit Sequence Number, a 32-bit Seed and a 32-bit Auth Key, which is the ISAAC output for that sequence number. The MD5 format is 24 bytes and the SHA-1 format is 28 bytes, and both are checked as described in RFC 5880.

The Auth Key does not cover any hash of the BFD Control Packet. The rest of the packet is completely unauthenticated in this mode, so the ISAAC format MUST NOT be used to signal state changes.
sections.eli5: The light message has a sticker with a counter, a random starting number, and the secret number for that count. The sticker proves who sent it, but it says nothing about the rest of the letter.

sections.title: Switching Between Strong and Light Modes
sections.content:
A session starts with the relevant Auth Type and the Optimized Authentication Mode set to 1. State transitions need full packet integrity checks, so the first Up packet MUST use mode 1, and each side keeps using the intensive method until the other side confirms the Up state with a packet that also uses it. Only after that MAY the sender move to mode 2.

There is no negotiation. The sender simply starts sending mode 2 packets, and a receiver switches when it sees mode 2 while it does not yet know the receive key. The current sequence numbers carry over into the new mode.

Moving back is allowed at any time by setting the mode field from 2 to 1. The RFC RECOMMENDS that implementations periodically switch to the intensive type for packets that keep the session Up, with an interval long enough that ISAAC still pays off. Sequence numbers keep increasing during such a switch, so ISAAC must keep generating pages to be ready to validate packets later.
sections.eli5: You start with the secret handshake, then switch to quick waves once both sides agree things are fine. Now and then you shake hands again to be sure.

sections.title: Secret Key and Seeding ISAAC
sections.content:
The secret key MUST be at least 8 octets long and SHOULD NOT exceed 128 octets. The security section RECOMMENDS 16 octets or more. A session MUST NOT change its Auth Key ID, and to rotate keys the BFD session has to be administratively disabled so the new session is seeded afresh.

ISAAC is seeded from a buffer filled with repeated copies of a structure holding the Seed, the Your Discriminator value, the secret key and a counter that starts at zero. The Seed MUST come from a CSPRNG and a new one MUST be created each time the session enters the Up state. It then stays fixed until another state change. Together the Seed and Your Discriminator add 64 bits of entropy, 32 from each party, which acts like a nonce against offline dictionary attacks.

Each direction has its own ISAAC instance, because the inputs differ on each side. The RFC includes test inputs and the first eight expected outputs for checking an implementation.
sections.eli5: Both friends mix the shared secret with two fresh random numbers, one from each, so the list of secret numbers is different for every conversation.

sections.title: Pages of Secret Numbers
sections.content:
ISAAC produces numbers in pages of 256 32-bit values. The receiver subtracts the base sequence number of the current page from a packet's sequence number to find which entry to expect, so lost packets are handled by simple arithmetic. The expensive mixing step runs only once per 256 packets.

Calculating the next page is destructive to the current one, so the RFC RECOMMENDS keeping both a current and a next page and computing the next page in the background. At 60 packets per second there are about four seconds to do so, and an attacker who spoofs packets cannot force the receiver to do heavy work in the fast path. A received packet must have a sequence number between bfd.RcvAuthSeq+1 and bfd.RcvAuthSeq+(3*Detect Mult), the right Seed and the right Auth Key, or it is discarded. The document makes no provision for losing more than 512 packets, so Detect Mult must be kept small enough.
sections.eli5: The secret numbers come in booklets of 256. Both friends know which page number they are on, so even if they miss a few shouts they can find their place.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
The RFC is frank about the weak spots. Security depends on ISAAC, which has had minimal analysis, and no proof is offered. ISAAC was chosen because many target systems lack hardware crypto assistance. Where block cipher hardware exists it offers no advantage, and the RFC names AES in OFB mode and ChaCha (RFC 8439) as alternatives. It calls ISAAC at best tolerable here and completely unsuitable for any other IETF protocol.

An attack would need the attacker to be on-path and active, to have packet contents, and to have deduced the secret key. If ISAAC is subverted, the periodic strong reauthentication limits how long a session is wrongly kept Up. Using the same key for ISAAC and for MD5 or SHA-1 means a recovered ISAAC key would compromise those too, so the RFC leaves the choice to the operator and RECOMMENDS that implementations allow distinct keys.

Random numbers such as the Seed SHOULD come from a non-ISAAC CSPRNG, and MUST come from a different source than the ISAAC generator for Auth Keys.
sections.eli5: This trick is a clever shortcut but not the strongest lock, and the authors say so. Use it only for the small waves and keep the strong lock for the important things.

fields.name: Auth Len
fields.desc: Length of the section in bytes.

fields.name: Auth Key ID
fields.desc: Which secret key is in use.

fields.name: Sequence Number
fields.desc: Incremented by one on every packet sent.

fields.name: Seed
fields.desc: Random value used with the shared key to initialize ISAAC.

fields.name: Auth Key
fields.desc: ISAAC output for this sequence number.
